text: Fatigue failure: from small cracks to sudden fracture.
First, we explain the science.
Then, we apply it to a bicycle crank.
Metals can fail under repeated loading, even when stress stays below yield strength.
One safe-looking load does not mean thousands of repeated loads are safe.
This real titanium specimen shows a crack starting at a defect.
Scratches, holes, and sharp corners can also concentrate stress.
First, a small crack starts.
Repeated loads can then extend it.
As the crack grows, less intact metal carries the load.
Finally, the remaining section breaks rapidly.
Damage builds gradually; the last break looks sudden.
An S-N curve connects stress amplitude with cycles to failure.
Amplitude is half the stress range.
The horizontal axis is logarithmic: each step means ten times more cycles.
Follow three hundred megapascals across to the curve, then down: ten thousand cycles.
At one hundred eighty megapascals, read one million cycles.
Lower amplitude gives longer life under the same conditions.
These numbers are illustrative, not crank measurements.
Real test results scatter.
Some steels show a fatigue limit; aluminum alloys generally have no clear limit.
Fracture toughness means resistance to fracture from an existing crack.
K_I describes crack-tip loading.
K_Ic is the material's plane-strain fracture toughness under valid conditions.
Here, Y is a geometry factor, sigma is stress, and a is crack length.
This formula estimates the stress intensity factor.
Keep crack length fixed and increase stress: K_I rises.
Keep stress fixed and lengthen the crack: K_I usually rises.
With linear elasticity and plane strain, rapid fracture may occur when maximum K_I reaches K_Ic.
Fatigue cracks can still grow below this critical value.
Why can a bicycle crank suddenly break after repeated pedaling?
This arm transfers pedal force to the drivetrain.
Each stroke changes the load.
Pedal threads, axle connections, scratches, and sharp corners can concentrate stress.
This real broken crank shows fatigue growth and final fracture.
A small crack can grow over many uses.
Higher amplitude usually shortens fatigue life.
Longer cracks raise stress intensity, making rapid fracture possible.
Protect surfaces, notice changes, and check for cracks.
Stop using a suspect part.
